comments.author: @IceMetalPunk
comments.text: Once GPT-4V is available via API (which I thought they already said would be in November?), the next thing is to get audio modality. The current "GPT can hear" feature is really just Whisper speech-to-text being passed into GPT's context, which means anything that's not speech gets lost, and any speech that's hard to transcribe (say, because multiple people are talking over each other) also gets lost. What we need is a true audio modality for GPT the way it now has vision -- passing audio tokens directly into the main transformer during training and inference -- so it can truly hear the world. The Suno Bark version of Whisper, if you like analogies 😁 I imagine with the same network learning from pictures, text, AND audio, it will be able to integrate and extract so much more understanding of the world, in a more grounded way than many AI-detractors think is even possible.

comments.author: @fusseldieb
comments.text:
The biggest road-block for building mind-boggling AI application has always been cost and memory.

Chatbots are a dumb, but wonderful example for this. Every interaction you need to include the initial prompt and the past 5-10 chats for it to remember. Then have a short chat with it to test and you can see a couple of cents vanishing from your account. That's bad. Imagine wanting to build any decent service out of this. You'll go bankrupt as soon as you open it to the public. Unless you do it with GPT-3.5, but it's not really the brightest in a lot of things.

Another great example are documents. Even when providing vector search and include snippets for it to use, including these snippets every interaction consumes a lot of tokens, and a lot of the time the vector search doesn't pop up with all the revelant infos, making it either hallucinate things that it doesn't know, or, straight up being dumb when answering a simple document question. I've even tried to do hybrid search, which uses vector proximity but also word similarity (character-based). It kinda sucks. The only solution is to include the whole document when requested in a 32k window or similar, but, as always, that uses a lot of tokens.

If OpenAI manages to store past informations somehow, and only counting new tokens, it would open up so much more possibilities.

comments.author: @Sgrunterundt
comments.text:
It is interesting how LLM agents (can) have three levels of memory, and it seems quite analogous to how my own brain works. There is the short term memory of the prompt context window. Fast, but limited and expensive at run time. 

It can have a long term memory in terms of data files that can be retrieved with function calls. Cheap to store a lot of data, but requires good indexing and costly to bring the relevant bits into short term memory. Things you have to think to recall, or maybe books and notes.

And then there is the stuff that has been learned completely. Knowledge that is in the guts. Knowledge in the weights and biases of the network itself. Things like strong associations and language skills themselves. Cheap and fast at runtime, but takes a long time and training to get it there.

Paying to fine-tune a model is basically telling it: "I don't want to have to tell you this all the time, go and study it until you know it in your sleep."

comments.author: @googleuser9592
comments.text: Read those 2 lines again. They aren't decreasing the cost at all, rather they are possibly adding "memory" capability so that you don't have to resend the chat history with every single prompt - THAT in turn will allow your follow-up prompts to be smaller, that's how you save money. The amount you would save would depend on how much this memory feature means to you. For some applications that don't use "memory" altogether (e.g. a business name generator) the new memory feature will save nothing, whereas a chat application that sends the entire chat history with every prompt can see a 100x decrease in price on long conversations! For example, if the first chat-response was 1000 tokens, followed by 100 more chat-responses each being 10 tokens large. The total cost without the new memory would accumulate to 150,500 tokens, but with the new memory feature it would cost 2,000 tokens total (1,000 for the first chat-response + a total of 1,000 (10 x 100) for the next 100 chat-responses), since it does not need to resend the first 1000-token chat-response with every subsequent message. That's a 75x price decrease in this example! Makes sense?
